claims.sentence: Quoting a real source does not guarantee support either: in clinical question answering, one model quoted its sources verbatim for 98.0\% of its claims, but only 37.1\% were fully substantiated by those quotes, mostly because the claims added details the quotes did not contain \citep{zhang2026verifiable}.
claims.claim: In clinical QA, one model (claude-opus-5) gave verbatim quotes for 98.0% of its claims but only 37.1% were fully substantiated by them, mostly because claims contained content the quotes did not support (unsupported addition).
claims.excerpt: For instance, claude-opus-5 produces verbatim quotes for 98.0% of its claims, but fully substantiates only 37.1%. ... this drop-off is largely due to partial support, as opposed ... to a complete lack of evidence. ... Unsupported addition covers cases where the quote fully substantiates some, but not all, of the statements ... in the claim. ... The vast majority of claims fall in the unsupported addition category.
claims.location: p. 1, Abstract; p. 4, Sec. 4 overview; p. 5, Finding 2; Table 3 (p. 6)
claims.note: Minor, no change needed: 37.1% is the source's rate over all 658 claims (CCR, 244 fully supported); over the 645 verbatim-quoted claims the strict rate is 37.8% (Table 3). The abstract itself uses 37.1% in this sense. For claude-opus-5, Table 3 attributes 347 of 401 shortfall cases to unsupported addition, consistent with 'mostly'.
